paragraphs: Meachar sheggadela maalat hattepilla shennizzonim haelyonim vehattachtonim al yadah dehi ammudat berumo shel olam sheggam laolamot haelyonim yimmashek shepa al yadah, lekak hizhiru bazzohar haqqadosh lehitpallel belachash ad sheapillu azenayv lo tishmana qolo, vehattaam hu kede shello yitqanneu bah hachitzonim mechamat godel maaloteha, ukemo shekkatab rabbenu morenu harab chayyim veyittol za"l b"olat tamid" dap n"v ammud b vezeh leshono: "hattepilla enah nikneset beshum raqia ki im otah tepilla dela ishtemaat leudenin, velaken biqriat shema tiqqenu sheyyashmia leazenayv, abal haka im hattepilla nishmaat leazenayv la saleqa, ki shomein hachitzonim umitarebin bahadah, ukeshehi belachash deenah nishmaat leazenayv az hi ruchanit meod miggeder teba rucha adam shehi penimit veruchanit yoter meod min hassitra achara ulekak en roin otah, vezeh hepek sebarat mhry"q bebet yosep sheppasaq sheyyoter tob lishmia leazenayv, veayyen babbarayta ubirushalmi vetimtza kidbaray hepek sebarato, veken haqqore beseper tora chad qare vechad sheteq, vei tere qeren gara mehemanuta, ki hattepilla uqeriat seper tora kullehu havu mealema illaa, dilgabbeh anachnu matztzelin belachash veku'" ad kan leshono ayyen sham:

clarification.explanation: Since the merit of prayer is so great — it nourishes the upper and lower worlds together, and constitutes a kind of pillar supporting the world — the holy Zohar warned that one should pray in a whisper, so that even the person himself cannot hear his own voice. The reason: so that the forces of impurity (the "outer ones") will not become jealous of the prayer because of its great greatness. Rabbi Chaim Vital explains that prayer does not ascend to any firmament unless it is inaudible to the ears — for if it is heard, the outer forces hear it, intermingle with it, and thereby blemish its sanctity. This view of Rabbi Chaim Vital stands against the view of the Maharik (cited in Beit Yosef), who ruled the opposite — that it is preferable for the prayer to be heard by the ears; but our teacher notes that the Baraita and the Yerushalmi prove in accordance with the words of Rabbi Chaim Vital, and not the view of the Maharik. By contrast, in the recitation of the Shema one must make it heard to the ears specifically, because there the situation is different. The reading of the Torah is likewise conducted this way: one reads aloud and one is silent (rather than two reading together, which is considered a defect in faithfulness), because both prayer and the Torah reading belong to the supernal world, in relation to which one must pray specifically in a whisper.
takeaways: One should recite the silent prayer (Amidah) so that even he himself does not hear his own voice, so that the forces of impurity will not intermingle with the prayer because of its great greatness.

There are those who disagree (the Maharik, in Beit Yosef), holding the opposite — that it is preferable for the prayer to be heard by the ears; but the Baraita and the Yerushalmi support the view of Rabbi Chaim Vital, that one should pray in complete whisper.
This differs from the recitation of the Shema, in which one must make it heard to the ears.
In the Torah reading as well, the practice is that only one reads aloud while another is silent, for a similar reason.

paragraphs: Velihyot ki hattepilla qedushshatah gedola meod vehi debarim haomedim berumo shel olam, lekak tzarik lehizzaher bah leomerah begup naqi vetahor, sheim haya tzarik linqabayv al yitpallel ad sheyyipneh, mishshum shenneemar "hikkon liqrat eloheka yisrael" (amos d, yb), veim hitpallel tepillato toeba vetzarik lachazor lehitpallel, bammeh debarim amurim bigdolim abal lo biqtannim, veen tzarik lachazor ella kesheeno yakol lehaamid atzmo shiur parsa shehu shaa vechomesh shaa, deqim lehu lachakamenu za"l kol shello yukal laatzor shiur zeh kebar nehpak hammaakol bemeayv lihyot tzoa gemura uketib "vekol qerabay et shem qadesho" (tehillim qg, ), ulepikak tepillato toeba vetzarik lachazor ulehitpallel, abal im yakol lehaamid atzmo shiur parsa yatza bediabad, veayyen "nishmat adam" kelal g' ot ' umikkol maqom lekattechilla tzarik lachush shello yitpallel begup meshuqqatz, apillu im yaabor zeman tepilla im yamtin ad sheyyipneh, vahagam deyakol lehaamid atzmo yoter mishshiur parsa, veha denaqeti chaza"l shiur happarsa behilluk haynu lehachmir, dehannitzrak linqabayv im yosheb yukal lehaamid atzmo yoter mishshiur mehallek veayyen "erek hashshulchan":

clarification.explanation: Because of the great sanctity of prayer, one must be careful to say it with a clean and pure body — one who needs to relieve himself should not pray until he has done so, as it is said, "Prepare to meet your God, O Israel." If he prayed nonetheless, his prayer is "an abomination" and he must go back and pray again — but this ruling applies only to major needs, and only if he cannot hold himself for the duration of a "parsah" (an hour and a fifth of an hour — 72 minutes), because according to our Sages, after this time the food in his intestines has already turned into actual excrement, and then one cannot say "and all my innards [shall bless] His holy name" over him. If he can hold himself for the duration of a parsah, he has fulfilled his obligation after the fact. But at the outset, one must be careful not to pray with a repulsive body even if this will cause him to be late for the time of prayer, and even if he is capable of holding himself longer than that measure — because the measure was set specifically with regard to walking, not with regard to sitting, in which one can hold himself for a longer time.
takeaways: One should not pray when in need of relieving himself; if he did pray nonetheless (for a major need, to the point that he cannot restrain himself for an hour and a fifth, that is, 72 minutes), he must go back and pray again.
At the outset, it is preferable to delay the time of prayer rather than to pray with an unclean body.

paragraphs: Im nitorer lo beemtza tepillato, ben ligdolim ben liqtannim, im yukal laatzor atzmo ad sheyyigmor tepillato- yigmor tepillato, veim lav muttar lo latzet ulepannot veachar kak yigmor tepillato, ki halika bilbad belo dibbur la chashiba hepseq, veraq demippene hakkabod hu en rauy sheyyapsiq beemtza tepillato, ubehay gavna shehu letzorek let lan bah:

clarification.explanation: If the need arises in the middle of prayer (whether major or minor) — if he can hold out until he finishes his prayer, he should finish it; and if not, he is permitted to go out and relieve himself and afterward complete his prayer, since walking alone without speech is not considered an interruption. The reason it is normally improper to interrupt prayer is a matter of respect (kavod), but where there is a genuine need there is no problem with it.
takeaways: If a need arises in the middle of prayer, one may go out (without speaking) and complete the prayer afterward; walking alone is not considered an interruption.

paragraphs: Im tinoq tinnep betzoa beemtza tepilla veen lo dabar etzlo lekassoto, o apillu sheyyesh lo dabar lekassoto hinneh al kol panim yesh recha ra, hare zeh mitracheq arba ammot mimmaqom shekkala harecha o yatza lebayit acher, veim yesh acherim omedim sham umitpallelim gam ken, velo hirgishu betinnup zeh shettinnep hattinoq etzlam sham, im epshar lehodia lahem kede sheyyitrachaqu shello al yede hepseq bedibbur yodiem, veim i epshar lehodia lahem ella raq al yede hepseq bedibbur, muttar lo lehapsiq bedibbur kede lehatztzilam meissur deorayeta umutab sheyyaaseh hu issur derabbanan lehapsiq bedibbur betok hattepilla, mishsheyyaasu acherim issur deorayeta lehitpallel bemaqom metunnap veayyen "chayye adam" kelal k"h ot z' ubi"nishmat adam" sham ot ', vekol zeh hu betinnup deikka issur tora, abal im hattinoq hishtin delekka bazeh ella issur derabbanan, asur lehapsiq bedibbur ella hu yitracheq arba ammot veyigmor tepillato velaacherim shehem mitpallelim sham shello hirgishu lo yittappel bahem leharchiqam apillu al yede remez bitnuat yadayv, dilgabbe deyadam yesh lismok al mah shekkatab ha"magen abraham" siman "ch dlhrshb" en tzarik leharchiq beme raglayim, veayyen "chayye adam" kelal k"h ot v:

clarification.explanation: If an infant soiled itself with excrement in the middle of prayer and there is nothing available to cover the mess, or even if there is a cover but a foul odor still lingers — one should move four amot away from where the smell is or move to a different room. If there are other worshippers present who have not noticed the soiling — if it is possible to inform them without an interruption of speech (for instance, by a hint), he should do so; and if it is not possible to inform them except through actual speech, he is permitted to interrupt with speech in order to save them from a Torah-level prohibition (praying in a soiled place), since it is preferable for him to commit a rabbinic-level prohibition (an interruption of speech) rather than for them to commit a Torah-level prohibition. All of this applies specifically to soiling that involves a Torah-level prohibition; but if the infant merely urinated (only a rabbinic-level prohibition), it is forbidden to interrupt with speech — rather, he himself should move four amot away and finish his prayer, and as for the others who have not noticed, he should not trouble himself to move them away, not even by a hand gesture.
takeaways: Severe soiling (a Torah-level prohibition) that disturbs prayer: one is permitted to interrupt with speech to warn others where a hint will not suffice.
Minor soiling (urination, only a rabbinic-level prohibition): it is forbidden to interrupt with speech under any circumstance, including a hint to others — one should only move himself away.

paragraphs: Bitpilla eno poseq lo leqaddish velo liqdushsha vekayyotze, ella yishtoq vikavven lemah sheomer hashlicha tzibbur venechshab keoneh leinyan sheyyetze yede chobato beqaddish uqedushsha, veap al gab denechshab keoneh en zeh nechshab lo hepseq ubesipri haq' "mqbtzyl" katabti deim hu rachoq mishshelicha tzibbur veeno shomea mimmennu haqqaddish o haqqedushsha en tzarik lishtoq ella yitpallel kedarko:

clarification.explanation: In the middle of the Amidah, one does not pause for Kaddish, Kedushah, or the like — rather, one remains silent and directs one's attention to what the chazzan (prayer leader) is saying, and this is considered as actually answering, for purposes of fulfilling one's obligation in Kaddish and Kedushah; and although it is considered as answering, this is not considered an interruption. If the person praying is far from the chazzan and cannot hear the Kaddish or Kedushah from him, he need not remain silent at all, but should continue praying as usual.
takeaways: During the Amidah, one remains silent and directs attention to the chazzan's Kaddish/Kedushah (this counts as answering, without being considered an interruption).
One who is too far from the chazzan to hear him continues his own prayer as usual, without pausing.

paragraphs: En lehapsiq bedibbur beemtza tepillat haamida ella davqa bimqom sakkana, abal i lekka sakkana apillu bishbil mitzva, kegon lomar lattoqea berosh hashshana bitpillat lachash demusap shettaa besimane hatteqiot, en lehapsiq beemtza hattepilla bedibbur lehachazir lattoqea sheyyitqa kahogen, veayyen "keneset haggedola" veod acharonim, veha deshare lehapsiq bedibbur bimqom sakkana haynu heka dei epshar lehimmalet bilti dibbur, abal im yukal lehimmalet al yede hilluk sheyyelek mimmeqomo lemaqom acher, lo yapsiq bedibbur, veap al pi deshare lehapsiq bedibbur mippene hassakkana, mikkol maqom im epshar lo leqatztzer dehaynu sheyyomar techillat kol beraka vesopah, beopen sheyyigmor tepillato veyimmalet min hassakkana velo yitztarek lehapsiq bedibbur beemtza- shappir dame:

clarification.explanation: One must not interrupt with speech in the middle of the Amidah except specifically in a case of danger — even for the sake of a mitzvah (for instance, to alert the shofar-blower on Rosh Hashanah that he erred in the order of the blasts), one should not interrupt. Even the permission to interrupt in a case of danger is limited to a situation where it is not possible to escape without speech; if it is possible to escape by moving to another place (by walking alone), one should not interrupt with speech. And even when it is permitted to interrupt because of danger, if it is possible to shorten the prayer (saying only the beginning and end of each blessing) so as to finish and escape the danger without any interruption of speech at all — it is preferable to do so.
takeaways: Interrupting the Amidah with speech is permitted only in a case of genuine danger from which there is no other way to escape.
If one can escape merely by walking, or by shortening the prayer, that is preferable to an interruption of speech.

paragraphs: Asur ligor bepiv beodo mitpallel betinoq hashshocheq ap al gab dematrido bitpillato, ella bigmar habberaka yaaseh tenua beqol davqa, o yirmoz beyadayv kede sheyyishtoq, veim asa ken veodennu mesacheq umatrido yarchiq atzmo mimmennu velo yedabber kelum, dahalika bilbad eno hepseq, vekol shehu letzorek kehay gavna shari:

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to scold aloud an infant who is playing and disturbing the person praying, even if it disturbs the prayer — rather, at the end of the blessing he should make a vocal sound (not actual speech) or gesture with his hands so that the infant will be quiet. If, after doing so, the infant continues to disturb him, he should move away from him without speaking at all, since walking alone is not considered an interruption, and anything done for such a need is permitted.
takeaways: One must not scold aloud during prayer even at a disturbing infant; one may hint with a vocal sound or hand gestures at the end of a blessing, and if that does not help, move away from him.

paragraphs: Im hipsiq tepillato mechamat ones veshaha kede ligmor et kol hattepilla meroshah lesopah, hare zeh chozer larosh umeshaarin lepi hammitpallel:

clarification.explanation: If one interrupted his prayer due to circumstances beyond his control, and delayed for a period of time equal to that needed to complete the entire prayer from start to finish — he must go back and pray from the beginning, and this measure of time is calculated according to that particular person's own pace of prayer.
takeaways: A prolonged interruption (equal to the time of a complete prayer) due to circumstances beyond one's control requires starting the prayer over from the beginning.

paragraphs: Taa o neenas velo hitpallel yesh lo tashlumin, ak lo tiqqenu tashlumin ella lattepilla hassemuka leotah hattepilla, abal tepillot acherot shehipsid en lahem tashlumin, lepikak taa o neenas velo hitpallel shacharit mitpallel mincha shettayim, vekol taut shetztzarik lachazor baaburo chayyab lehashlim battepilla hassemuka kegon shehizkir geshem uberak alenu bizman haqqayitz, veken taut derosh chodesh vekayyotze bazeh. vaapillu beshabbat sheyyesh tepillat musap im kol zeh tepillat hammincha miqqere tepilla hassemuka leshacharit, mippene sheshshenehem bimqom hattemidin, abal musap hu qarebban acher laken tashlumin shel shacharit hu bemincha tamid apillu beshabbat veyom tob, ukesheoseh tashlumin leshacharit bemincha, yitpallel harishona mincha, vehashshenit letashlumin, veim hippek bekavvanato lo yatza yede tepilla shehi tashlumin, vetzarik lachazor lehitpallel otah, veken haddin bekol maqom shetztzarik lehitpallel tashlumin, siman laddabar baal habbayit veoreach niknasim labbayit, mi niknas techilla? baal habbayit niknas techilla: taa velo hitpallel mincha mitpallel arbit shettayim, taa velo hitpallel arbit mitpallel shacharit shettayim, dehaynu leachar sheamar qeriat shema utepillat shemoneh esreh, yomar "ashre" veachar kak yitpallel tashlume arbit, abal achar mincha en lomar "ashre" al pi hassod betorat chiyyub betiqqune hattepillot, lekak im mashlim shacharit achar mincha, o mincha achar arbit lo yomar "ashre" benetayim, raq yishheh kede hilluk arba ammot vekannizkar baacharonim:

clarification.explanation: One who erred or was prevented by circumstances beyond his control from praying has makeup prayers (tashlumin), but the Sages instituted makeup prayers only for the prayer adjacent to the one that was missed — not for other prayers that were lost. Therefore, one who missed Shacharit prays Minchah twice. Any error requiring repetition of the prayer (such as mentioning rain during the summer, or an error regarding Rosh Chodesh) is likewise made up in the adjacent prayer. Even on Shabbat, when there is also a Musaf prayer, the Minchah prayer is nonetheless considered the prayer "adjacent" to Shacharit (because both correspond to the Tamid offering), while Musaf is a separate offering; therefore the makeup for Shacharit is always done in Minchah, even on Shabbat and Yom Tov. When one makes up Shacharit in Minchah, he prays the first as the obligatory Minchah, and the second as the makeup; if he reversed his intention, he has not fulfilled the obligation of the makeup prayer and must repeat it. A sign to remember this: the homeowner enters before the guest. One who missed Minchah makes it up by praying Arvit twice; one who missed Arvit makes it up by praying Shacharit twice — that is, after reciting the Shema and the Amidah, he says "Ashrei" and then prays the makeup for Arvit. But after Minchah, one does not say "Ashrei," by mystical tradition, as a matter of the fixed order of the prayers; therefore, when making up Shacharit after Minchah, or Minchah after Arvit, one does not say "Ashrei" in between, but merely waits the time it takes to walk four amot.
takeaways: Makeup prayers (tashlumin) for a missed prayer are performed only in the adjacent prayer: a missed Shacharit is made up in Minchah; a missed Minchah, in Arvit; a missed Arvit, in Shacharit.
One must pray the regular obligatory prayer first and only afterward the makeup prayer — reversing the order invalidates the makeup.
After Minchah, when making up a different prayer before it, one does not say "Ashrei" in between — one only waits the time it takes to walk four amot.

paragraphs: Tzarik shebbihyoto asuq bitpilla, yitpallel tepilla haacheret lehashlim, velo yaaseh hapsaqa benetayim, sheim shaha harbeh achar shehitpallel tepilla shehi chobat otah shaa, eno yakol lehitpallel tashlumin tepilla shehipsid, lepi shello tiqqenu tashlumin lattepilla shehipsid ella bizman sheoseq bitpilla shehi chobat otah shaa, sheaz kevan shehu oseq bitpilla chozer umashlim mah sheppasha bitpillato:

clarification.explanation: In order for makeup prayers to take effect properly, one must pray the completing prayer immediately, adjacent to the obligatory prayer of that hour, without a significant pause in between. If one waited a long time after the obligatory prayer, he can no longer pray a makeup for the prayer he missed, because the institution of makeup prayers is valid only while one is still "engaged in prayer" (immediately following the obligatory prayer).
takeaways: Makeup prayers are valid only if recited immediately adjacent to the obligatory prayer, without a lengthy pause.

paragraphs: Shakach velo hitpallel shacharit umusap, venizkar bemincha yitpallel mincha techilla, veachareha musap veachar kak tashlumin deshacharit, veim hitpallel musap qodem mincha yatza, veim abar kol hayyom velo hitpallel musap en lah tashlumin, apillu betorat nedaba deabar zemanno batel qarebbano:

clarification.explanation: One who forgot and did not pray Shacharit and Musaf, and remembered at the time of Minchah, prays Minchah first, then Musaf, and afterward the makeup for Shacharit. If he prayed Musaf before Minchah, he has fulfilled his obligation. But if the entire day passed and he did not pray Musaf at all, there is no makeup for it in any manner, not even as a voluntary offering — because "once its time has passed, its offering is void."
takeaways: The order of making up a missed Shacharit and Musaf: Minchah, then Musaf, then the makeup for Shacharit.
A Musaf missed for the entire day has no makeup at all, not even as a voluntary prayer.

paragraphs: Mi shettaa velo hitpallel mincha beereb shabbat, mitpallel arbit shettayim shel shabbat, harishona learbit usheniyya letashlumin, veim taa velo hitpallel mincha beshabbat, mitpallel bemotzae shabbat arbit shettayim shel chol, umabdil barishona, veeno mabdil bashsheniyya, veim hibdil bishtehen, o lo hibdil beshum achat mehen yatza, abal im lo hibdil barishona vehibdil bashsheniyya az sheniyya aleta lo, verishona lo aleta lo, dekevan shello hibdil barishona gilla dato shehitpallel harishona letashlumin vezeh lo yoil kemo shekkatabti leel deen tashlumin ella bashsheniyya, veken im lo hitpallel mincha beereb rosh chodesh mitpallel arbit shettayim belel rosh chodesh, umazkir bishnehem yaaleh veyabo, veim lo hizkir barishona vehizkir bashsheniyya tzarik lachazor ulehitpallel, vekol zeh kesheasa ken bemezid, abal im asa beshogeg sheshshakach velo hizkir barishona en tzarik lachazor, hen bedin yaaleh veyabo veen bedin hahabdala hannizkar leel, vekol shekken im omer shebbashsheniyya nitkavven beperush letashlumin deen tzarik lachazor, veyesh omerim dehabdala shane dekol shello peresh beperush shehashsheniyya letashlumin tzarik lachazor, veyesh machmirim yoter behabdala daapillu perash name tzarik lachazor, hilkak haddin hu im shakach velo hibdil barishona lo yabdil bashsheniyya, veim taa chozer tepillat hachoba shel otah shaa abal shel tashlumin hoil vehukshera hukshera vekannizkar bechesed laalapim": veken mi sheshshakach o neenas velo hitpallel arbit lel shabbat qodesh, yitpallel shacharit shettayim veyomar bishtehen "yismach mosheh", vehu haddin beminchat shabbat sheyyitpallel bishtehen "atta echad", zeh hakkelal: kol tashlumin tihyeh kemo tepillat hachoba shel otah shaa shemmashlim bah, siman laddabar: oreach shennitaksen etzel baal habbayit, tzarik leekol mimmah sheokel baal habbayit, velo yebaqqesh leekol kepi hammaakol sheokel bebeto:

clarification.explanation:
One who erred and did not pray Minchah on Friday afternoon prays Arvit of Shabbat twice: the first for the obligation of Arvit and the second as the makeup. And if he did not pray Minchah on Shabbat, he prays Arvit of the weekday twice on Motza'ei Shabbat, reciting Havdalah ("Atah Chonantanu") in the first and not in the second. If he recited Havdalah in both, or in neither, he has fulfilled his obligation; but if he did not recite it in the first and did recite it in the second — the second counts for him and the first does not, since by not reciting Havdalah in the first he revealed his intent that he had prayed the first as the makeup, and there is no makeup except in the second [prayer].
Likewise, on the eve of Rosh Chodesh — one prays Arvit twice on the night of Rosh Chodesh, mentioning "Ya'aleh V'Yavo" in both; if he did not mention it in the first and did mention it in the second, he must go back and pray again. All of this applies when done deliberately; but when done unintentionally — forgetting to mention it in the first — he need not go back and pray again (neither in the law of Ya'aleh V'Yavo nor in the law of Havdalah mentioned above), and all the more so if he says he specifically intended the second to be the makeup. Some say that Havdalah is different — that whenever he did not specify that the second is the makeup, he must go back and pray again; and some are even more stringent about Havdalah, saying that even if he did specify, he must still go back. Therefore the practical ruling is: one who forgot and did not recite Havdalah in the first should not recite Havdalah in the second; and if he erred, he repeats the obligatory prayer of that hour, but the makeup prayer, since it was already validly performed, remains valid. Likewise, one who forgot or was prevented from praying Arvit on the night of Shabbat Kodesh prays Shacharit twice, saying "Yismach Moshe" in both, and the same for the Minchah of Shabbat, saying "Atah Echad" in both. The general rule: every makeup prayer follows the form of the obligatory prayer of the hour in which it is recited. A sign for this: a guest lodging with a homeowner eats from what the homeowner eats, and does not ask to eat the food he is accustomed to in his own home.
takeaways: One who forgot Minchah makes it up in the next prayer: the first recitation for the obligation, the second for the makeup.
On Motza'ei Shabbat: one recites Havdalah in the first prayer only; if he did not recite it in the first but did in the second, only the second counted.
The general rule: the makeup prayer takes the form of the obligatory prayer of the hour in which it is recited (Ya'aleh V'Yavo / Yismach Moshe / Atah Echad in both).

paragraphs: En tashlumin litpilla bitpillat hassemuka ella lemi shettaa o shakach o neenas, abal im hezid velo hitpallel tepilla achat en lah tashlumin kelal, veyesh petaim veen mitpallelim mincha bishat hannepesh al daat lehitpallel arbit shettayim, vetzarik lehazhir hamon haam bazeh:

clarification.explanation: Makeup prayers exist only for one who erred, forgot, or was prevented by circumstances beyond his control from praying — but for one who deliberately (intentionally) did not pray a particular prayer, there is no makeup at all. There are simple-minded people who deliberately do not pray Minchah, thinking to pray Arvit twice in its place — and the masses must be warned against this invalid practice.
takeaways: Makeup prayers are intended only for error, forgetfulness, or circumstances beyond one's control — not for one who deliberately missed a prayer.
It is forbidden to deliberately refrain from Minchah with the plan of making it up in Arvit — this does not have the validity of a proper makeup prayer.

paragraphs: Mi shello hitpallel beod sheyyesh lo zeman lehitpallel, mippene shessabur sheadayin yishshaer lo zeman achar sheyyigmor eseq shemmitasseq bo, uben kak uben kak abera lo hashshaa yesh omerim sheen lo tashlumin, lekak yitpallel tashlumin betorat nedaba, veyatneh veyomar im ani mechuyyab lehashlim betorat choba tihyeh tepilla zo tashlumin shel choba, veim en ani mechuyyab lehitpallel tashlumin shel choba yeqabbelenna hashshem yitbarak betorat nedaba, veyizzaher gam ken lechaddesh bah b"shomea tepilla" ezeh debar baqqasha sheen ragil lebaqqesho berob hayyamim, veayyen "chesed lealpayim": veken mi shennishtakker qodem shehiggia zeman tepilla venishar beshekkeroto velo hitpallel, chashib ones veyesh lah tashlumin, abal im nistakker achar zeman tepilla shehaya yakol lehitpallel qodem shikrut velo hitpallel, venishar beshekkeroto ad sheabar zeman tepilla, yesh omerim dela have ones veen lo tashlumin, veyesh omerim dachashib ones al ken yitpallel hattashlumin veyatneh qodem kaasher katabnu leel:

clarification.explanation: One who did not pray in the time available to him, believing that time would remain after finishing some other business, and in the end the time passed regardless — some say he has no ordinary makeup prayer. In such a case he should pray the makeup as a voluntary offering, stipulating: if he is obligated to make it up as an obligation, let this prayer be the obligatory makeup; and if he is not obligated, may the Blessed Name accept it as a voluntary offering. He should also introduce, in "Shome'a Tefillah," a special request that he does not customarily make every day (as a sign that this is a voluntary prayer and not an ordinary obligation). Likewise, one who became drunk before the time for prayer and remained drunk is considered to have been prevented by circumstances beyond his control, and has a makeup prayer; but one who became drunk after he was already able to pray, and did not pray, and remained drunk until the time passed — there is a dispute as to whether this is considered as being so prevented: some say it is not, and therefore there is no makeup; and some say it is, and therefore he should pray the makeup and stipulate as stated above.
takeaways: One who missed a prayer due to a mistaken assumption that time would remain, prays the makeup conditionally ("if obligated - as an obligation, if not - as a voluntary offering"), with a renewed request in "Shome'a Tefillah."
Drunkenness: if it occurred before the time for prayer, it is considered complete circumstances beyond one's control, with a makeup prayer; if after he could already have prayed, there is a dispute.

paragraphs: Mi shehaya tarud betzorek mamono shello yabo lide hepsed min haqqeren, veal yede ken hipsid millehitpallel yesh lo tashlumin, ak vadday lo tob asa lehaabir zeman tepilla mishshum hepsed mamon:

clarification.explanation: One who was occupied with an urgent monetary matter in order to avoid a financial loss, and as a result missed a prayer, has a makeup prayer. But he certainly did not act properly in letting the time for prayer pass out of concern for money.
takeaways: Urgent monetary preoccupation that caused a missed prayer entitles one to a makeup prayer, but this is not a proper thing to do in the first place.

paragraphs: En mitpallelin tepillat nedaba beshabbat veyom tob velaken kol heka dehaddin hu sheyyachazor lehitpallel betorat nedaba, o heka deamerinan missapeq yitpallel veyatneh kannizkar leel, en mitpallelin kazot beshabbat veyom tob, al ken heka dechal rosh chodesh yom shishshi vehu yom echad davqa, veshakach lehazkir rosh chodesh bammincha venizkar achar shechasheka, veken im taa bemincha deyom acharon shel chol hammoed deballayla hu yom tob, bekol zeh lo yitpallel tepillat hattashlumin mishshum dehaddin bazeh lachazor betorat nedaba, veen mitpallelin nedaba beshabbat veyom tob veayyen "machaziq beraka":

clarification.explanation: One does not pray a voluntary prayer on Shabbat and Yom Tov. Therefore, in any case where the law requires a makeup as a voluntary offering, or where one must pray out of doubt with a stipulation (as mentioned above), this should not be done on Shabbat and Yom Tov. For example: if Rosh Chodesh falls on Friday (a single day) and one forgot to mention Rosh Chodesh in Minchah and remembered only after Shabbat had gone out, or if one erred in the Minchah of the last day of Chol HaMoed (when that night is already Yom Tov) — in these cases one should not pray the makeup, because the law requires a voluntary prayer, and one does not pray a voluntary prayer on Shabbat and Yom Tov.
takeaways: There is no voluntary prayer on Shabbat and Yom Tov; any case where the law requires a makeup as a voluntary offering or out of doubt cannot be fulfilled on these days — rather, the makeup is forgone.

paragraphs: Hattoeh umazkir meora shear yamim bitpilla shello bizmannah bemidi deen lo shayyakut bazzeman hahu, ap al gab deikka disbira lehu dachashib kesach benetayim, mikkol maqom bediabad yesh lismok al happoseqim disbira lehu la have hepseq veayyen" yosep ometz" siman Adonai "vechesed laalapim" siman q"ch:

clarification.explanation: One who mistakenly mentions, within his prayer, an occurrence belonging to a different day out of its proper time (something unrelated to that time) — even though some hold this is considered like an interruption of speech, nevertheless, after the fact, one may rely on the poskim who hold that this is not considered an interruption.
takeaways: Mistakenly mentioning an irrelevant occurrence within the prayer does not invalidate it after the fact, according to the majority of poskim.

paragraphs: Im leachar shehitpallel hattashlumin nizkar shettaa bitpilla rishona beopen shehaddin hu shetztzarik lachazor, chozer gam hattashlumin betorat nedaba, chutz mishshabbat veyom tob, deen tepillat nedaba beshabbat veyom tob vekannizkar leel:

clarification.explanation: If, after already having prayed the makeup prayer, one remembers that he had also erred in the first prayer in a way that requires repeating it — he must also repeat the makeup prayer, as a voluntary offering, except on Shabbat and Yom Tov, when there is no voluntary prayer at all, as mentioned above.
takeaways: An error discovered in the first prayer after the makeup has already been completed requires repeating the makeup as well (as a voluntary offering, except on Shabbat and Yom Tov).

paragraphs: Im hitchil lehitpallel al daat shello hitpallel, venizkar shekkebar hitpallel, poseq apillu beemtza habberaka, vela mehanne chiddush vesheyyachshob betorat nedaba, hoil vehitchil battechilla addata dechoba, vehu haddin im chazar hattepilla al dabar sheen tzarik lachazor min haddin baaburo, venizkar beemtza hattepilla shettaa baddin hare zeh poseq apillu beemtza habberaka:

clarification.explanation: If one began to pray thinking he had not yet prayed, and in the middle remembered that he had actually already prayed — he must stop immediately, even in the middle of a blessing, and it does not help to think of the prayer as a voluntary offering and continue, since he began it from the outset with the intent of an obligation. The same rule applies if he repeated a prayer for a reason that did not, according to the strict law, require repetition, and remembered in the middle that he had erred in his judgment — he must stop even in the middle of a blessing.
takeaways: One who mistakenly began praying (thinking he had not yet prayed, or thinking he needed to repeat) and remembers in the middle that he erred, must stop immediately, even in the middle of a blessing.

paragraphs: Im nitbalbel beemtza tepillato veeno yodea hekan hu omed, chozer lerosh hattepilla, bammeh debarim amurim? im nitbalbel ad shello siyyem shelosha rishonot, abal im barur lo shessiyyem shelosha rishonot karauy venitbalbel baemtzaiyyot, deeno yodea im hu omed b"atta chonen" o besheachareha, chozer l"atta chonen", veim barur lo al beraka min haemtzaiyyot sheamarah kahogen vechatam bah, az chozer labberaka shehi achar otah beraka shebbarur lo sheamarah kullah kahogen veayyen "chesed laalapim":

clarification.explanation: One who becomes confused in the middle of his prayer and does not remember where he is, goes back to the beginning of the prayer — but only if he had not yet finished the first three blessings. If it is clear to him that he finished the first three properly, and he became confused among the middle blessings (not remembering whether he is at "Atah Chonen" or the blessing after it), he goes back to "Atah Chonen." And if he clearly recalls finishing a certain one of the middle blessings and beginning another — he goes back to the blessing following the last one he is certain he recited in full, properly.
takeaways: Confusion before finishing the first three blessings — one returns to the beginning of the prayer.
Confusion among the middle blessings — one returns to "Atah Chonen," unless he clearly remembers that a particular blessing was said in full, in which case he continues from the blessing after it.

paragraphs: Shelicha tzibbur shettaa bitpillat lachash beopen shetztzarik lachazor, yotze yede chobato bammeh shechozer hattepilla beqol ram, veen tzarik lachazor ulehitpallel belachash:

clarification.explanation: A prayer leader who erred in his silent Amidah in a way that the law requires repetition fulfills his obligation through his repetition of the prayer aloud (the Chazarat HaShatz — the reader's repetition), and need not go back and pray silently again separately.
takeaways: A chazzan who erred in the silent Amidah fulfills his obligation through the loud repetition (Chazarat HaShatz), and need not repeat it silently separately.

paragraphs: Bazzeman hazzeh en mitpallelin nedaba ella raq leet hatztzorek mah shemmukrach lehitpallel mishshurat haddin, deen leb haadam mekavven yapeh merosh vead sop, veqarenan beh "lamma li rob zibchakem" (yeshaya , y), vehalvay sheyyukal lehitpallel bitpillot hachoba karauy bekavvanat halleb:

clarification.explanation: In our time, we do not pray voluntary prayers, but only pray what is obligatory by strict law and as needed — because a person's heart is not properly focused from the beginning of the prayer to its end, and of this it is said, "Why do I need your many sacrifices?" Rabbi Yosef Chaim concludes with the hope that a person will merit, at the very least, to pray the ordinary obligatory prayers properly, with intention of the heart.
takeaways: In our time we do not pray voluntary prayers at all, but only the obligatory prayers required by Torah and rabbinic law.
Rabbi Yosef Chaim hopes that at least the obligatory prayers themselves be said with genuine intention of the heart.
